title: True words aren't pretty
hookLine: true words aren't beautiful; the more the sage gives, the more he has (Tao Te Ching 81)

cards: Two notes after a job interview. One is from a recruiter: wonderful energy, so impressive, we'll be in touch.
The other is from an old friend who looked at your answers: the second one rambled, and you never said why you want the job. One is lovely to read. The other is the one you'll actually use.
Chapter eighty-one of the Tao Te Ching opens with that difference, and then, almost in the same breath, it turns to giving.

teach.b: First, the opening pair. Words that are true aren't pretty, the chapter says, and pretty words aren't true. It's a mirror line: turn it around and it still holds.
That doesn't mean every kind word is a lie.
It means polish isn't the same thing as truth, and sometimes the polish is there to cover something. Second, two more pairs in the same shape. The good don't argue, and those who argue aren't good.
Those who really know aren't widely learned, and the widely learned don't really know. These sound harsh until you remember chapter seventy-one, where the best knowing was knowing you don't know.
Piling up facts and winning debates are both set to one side. Third, the turn, where our line comes from. The sage doesn't hoard.
The more the sage does for others, the more the sage has.

teach.h: THE MORE HE GIVES, THE MORE HE HAS.
teach.b: The more the sage gives, the more the sage's own store grows. As arithmetic, it's nonsense.
As a life, it starts to make sense: a teacher who explains a thing understands it better; a cook who feeds people gets a full table. Fourth, the closing lines.

teach.h: BENEFIT, DON'T HARM. ACT, DON'T FIGHT.
teach.b: Heaven's way is to benefit and not harm.
The sage's way is to act and not contend.
After all the water, valleys and uncarved wood, the chapter settles on giving without fighting: the plain sentence instead of the shiny one, the thing handed over without a receipt.

how: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter eighty-one as a summary of the sage's way: speak plainly, don't argue for the sake of winning, don't hoard, and find that giving to others leaves you with more.

games.q: what does “true words aren't pretty” mean?
o: plain speech is rude, so the wise say very little at all
honest words often lack polish, and polish can hide the truth
only harsh words can be trusted, so kindness is a lie

games.q: the last chapter's pairs: tap them.

s: chapter eighty-one says every kind word is a lie
it says pretty words aren't true. polish isn't the same as truth; that's different from calling kindness false.
the chapter says the sage doesn't hoard
the sage doesn't store up; the more the sage gives to others, the more the sage has.
chapter eighty-one ends on winning arguments
it ends: heaven's way is to benefit and not harm; the sage's way is to act and not contend.

games.q: you're the sage. you have plenty, and people keep asking. what does chapter eighty-one say happens?
o: you store it up, so there's enough for later.
the more you give, the more you have.
you give until there's nothing left.
games.why: the sage doesn't hoard. the more the sage does for others, the more the sage has; the more the sage gives, the more the sage's store grows.

practice: Look around your life for one thing someone else could use: a coat in the closet, a finished book, an hour, a skill like fixing a bike or reading a lease, or a true word someone needs, said plainly and kindly.
Pick one and picture handing it over. Then notice what's left in your own hands afterward.

wordCard.voice: True words aren't pretty. Chapter eighty-one: true words aren't beautiful, and beautiful words aren't true; the more the sage gives, the more the sage has. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese: true words aren't beautiful, the opening of chapter eighty-one.

carryVoice: Your line: the more I give. A plain, true word counts as a gift, too. I'll be here tomorrow.
